lesson.title: Carbon's Special Talent: The Foundation of Organic Chemistry
lesson.summary: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon-based molecules, and carbon's unique bonding versatility, the four covalent bonds it can form in countless combinations, is what makes the staggering diversity of life's molecules possible.
lesson.body:
Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry devoted to compounds built around carbon atoms, and it exists as its own field because carbon behaves so differently from nearly every other element on the periodic table. Recall from atomic structure that carbon has six protons and, more importantly for chemistry, four electrons in its outermost shell. Recall also from covalent bonding that atoms share pairs of electrons to fill their outer shells and become stable. With exactly four valence electrons to share, a carbon atom can form four separate covalent bonds at once, more shared connections than almost any other common element manages.

This bonding capacity is what makes carbon uniquely suited to building large, complex molecules. A carbon atom can bond to four different atoms simultaneously, including other carbon atoms, and those carbon atoms can in turn bond to still more carbons, generating long chains, branched structures, and closed rings. Carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen covalent bonds are also strong enough to be stable under the conditions found in living cells, so once a carbon skeleton is assembled it does not spontaneously fall apart, yet the bonds are not so strong that enzymes cannot rearrange them when the cell needs to build or break down a molecule. That balance, stable but not inert, is exactly what a chemistry of life requires.

The simplest organic molecule, methane, illustrates the basic geometry: one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms, each connection a single covalent bond, arranged so the hydrogens point toward the corners of a tetrahedron around the central carbon. Real biological molecules build on this same logic at a much larger scale. Glucose, for example, has a backbone of six carbon atoms that, in its most common form, closes into a six-membered ring, with additional atoms and groups attached around that ring. Whether a carbon skeleton takes the shape of a straight chain, a branch, or a ring, it is the carbon-to-carbon backbone that provides the underlying structural framework everything else attaches to.

Because carbon can link up in so many different arrangements, and because those arrangements can include double and even triple bonds between carbons for additional rigidity or reactivity, the number of possible organic molecules is effectively unlimited. Two molecules can even share the exact same atoms in the exact same ratio, called isomers, yet behave completely differently in a cell simply because those atoms are arranged differently around the carbon skeleton. This is the reason carbon, rather than any other element, ended up as the backbone of every major class of biological macromolecule: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids are all, at their core, carbon skeletons decorated with other atoms.

A bare carbon skeleton on its own, though, is chemically fairly bland; a chain of pure carbon and hydrogen atoms does not dissolve well in water and does not react easily with much of anything, which is not very useful for the dynamic chemistry of a living cell. What actually gives an organic molecule its specific chemical personality, its polarity, its acidity, its reactivity, is the particular small clusters of atoms attached to that carbon backbone, and that is exactly the subject of functional groups, covered next.
